figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Resistance-guided discovery of novel genetic pathways for antibiotic inhibitors of peptide deformylase. (a) Actinonin and matlystatin are
established antibiotic inhibitors of bacterial peptide deformylase (PDF). Both feature a hydroxamate that chelates a metal ion in the PDF active site.
(b) ClusterScout was used to find biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) with nonribosomal peptide (NRPS) genes colocalized with an additional
genomic copy of PDF, which may provide protection against nascent PDF inhibitory natural products. A BGC alignment was generated using
CORASON. These BGCs have varying similarity to the pathways for actinonin and matlystatin. (c) A candidate BGC from Gammaproteobacteria
was selected for further analysis. Plasmids were designed to enable heterologous expression in E. coli strain BAP1. (d) Molecular networking
between a fractionated V. tubiashii extract and an extract from our heterologous expression strain identified a small series of peptides with apparent
similarity to the annotated leucine-valine dipeptide. (e) Extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) of the two dominant ions identified in our molecular
networking analysis, along with a base peak chromatogram (BPC) of the associated E. coli culture extract.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Structures of BGC products and biosynthesis by an unusual
trans-acting N-methyltransferase. (a) The absolute structures of 1 and
2 were established by NMR and total synthesis. (b) The substrate
preference of the N-methyltransferase was assessed using N-acetyl-
cysteamine (SNAC) analogs of biosynthetic intermediates. BPCs of
enzymatic reactions are depicted (black) alongside EICs of unreacted
(magenta) and methylated (cyan) SNAC peptides. This enzyme
preferentially N-methylates polyketide-extended tripeptide SNACs.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Metabolomic analysis of antibacterial extracts. (a) Spot-on-
lawn assays show that V. ordalii 12B09 (BGC+) inhibits V.
crassostreae, while a BGC-knockout and V. tubiashii do not. (b)
Molecular networking of extracts from four bacteria carrying the BGC
reveal a series of new metabolites related to 1, seen in V. ordalii 12B09
and P. asymbiotica. (c) EICs of the new ions identified in a
fractionated extract from V. ordalii 12B09, including the isolated
active molecule, 4.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Structure and biosynthesis of gammanonin. The gam BGC
encodes an NRPS-PKS assembly line with a unique reductase (RE)
domain, along with the trans-acting N-methyltransferase GamE, self-
protection PDF GamD, and GamF PPTase. GamE acts primarily on
the polyketide-extended tripeptide. Given the abundance of 4 in
extracts and the dissimilarity of the RE domain, hemiaminal formation
may be assisted by the enzyme during release from the PKS.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Inhibition of PDF enzymes by gammanonin. Purified PDF
enzymes were used in a fluorescamine assay, measuring release of a
free amine from a formylated peptide substrate. 100 μM gammanonin
(GAM) was assayed against 100 μM actinonin, alongside negative
(DTT) and positive (DMSO) controls. Statistically significant
inhibition was seen against PDFs from (a) E. coli, (b) V. crassostreae,
and (c) V. tubiashii. The BGC-associated PDF enzyme GamD (d)
demonstrated a degree of resistance to the effects of gammanonin
treatment. Error bars represent mean with standard deviation. Data
points represent biological replicates from a representative experi-
ment. Statistical significance determined by two-tailed Student’s t test.
